# TEAM FORTRESS 2 IS THE UNSTOPPABLE FORCE OF GAMING  There are games that are released. There are games that become popular. There are games that become classics. And then there is Team Fortress 2, a game that somehow escaped the normal cycle of entertainment and became something completely different. It is not simply a product made to be consumed and forgotten. It is a place, a memory, a never-ending source of chaos that somehow becomes more impressive the longer it exists.  Team Fortress 2 does not feel like a game created by a company. It feels like something that was discovered. Like someone opened a door and accidentally found an entire universe filled with impossible moments, ridiculous situations, and endless reasons to laugh. It feels less like software and more like a machine designed specifically to generate unforgettable experiences.  The greatest mystery about TF2 is that absolutely everything about it should be impossible. The combination of absurd humor, serious competitive gameplay, completely ridiculous weapons, unpredictable physics, and a community that refuses to behave normally should not create something so perfect. Yet somehow, it does. Somehow, every strange piece fits together like it was always meant to exist.  Team Fortress 2 does not need to be realistic because realism was never the goal. It achieved something much harder: identity. Thousands of games can look realistic. Thousands can have bigger explosions, higher resolutions, and more advanced technology. But very few can make you recognize them instantly from a single sound, a single animation, or a single ridiculous situation.  You know when you hear a certain voice line.  You know when you see a certain movement.  You know when something completely absurd is about to happen.  That is TF2.  It has a personality so powerful that it feels like the game itself has a sense of humor.  Even after all these years, Team Fortress 2 continues to exist in a way that feels almost impossible. Time has tried to move forward, but TF2 simply refused to follow. It stayed exactly where it needed to be: a perfect combination of chaos and creativity. It does not chase every new trend. It does not need to. Trends come and go, but people still return to TF2 because there is nothing else that creates the same feeling.  The game does not create ordinary matches.  It creates stories.  A normal session can turn into something that sounds completely fictional. Someone performs a ridiculous move that should never have worked. Someone survives a situation that should have been impossible. Someone creates a moment so funny that everyone forgets they were even trying to win.  And that is the secret of TF2.  The objective might be to capture a point, push a cart, or defeat the enemy team, but the real objective is creating a moment worth remembering.  The game understands that the funniest and greatest moments are often the ones nobody planned.  That is why the chaos feels so natural.  The famous "bugs" and strange behaviors of TF2 are part of this legendary unpredictability. Other games try to hide their mistakes because they are afraid of losing control. Team Fortress 2 somehow turned losing control into one of its greatest strengths. When something unexpected happens, the game does not feel broken. It feels alive.  A physics interaction that makes absolutely no sense becomes a story.  A strange animation becomes a joke that survives for years.  A completely impossible situation becomes the reason someone remembers that match forever.  The game does not break reality.  It simply stretches reality until it becomes more entertaining.  The Source Engine has become almost mythical because of this. It feels like an ancient machine powered by forgotten knowledge, caffeine, and pure determination. Nobody looks at the Source Engine and thinks, "This behaves exactly as expected." They look at it and think, "I have no idea why this works, but I am grateful that it does."  And somehow, that uncertainty became part of the magic.  The classes themselves feel like they were created not just to fill roles, but to create completely different ways of experiencing chaos. Every person who joins a server finds their own way to become part of the madness. Some people become unstoppable forces. Some become unpredictable comedians. Some become legends because of one ridiculous moment that nobody else could have created.  That is what makes TF2 different.  The game does not demand that everyone play the same way.  It gives everyone a chance to create their own story.  The maps are not just places where battles happen. They become memories. They become locations where thousands of completely random moments happened and somehow became important. A simple corner of a map can become famous because of something ridiculous that happened there years ago. A random room can become a place where an entire community remembers a legendary event.  The same thing happens with the cosmetics. In many games, items are just decorations. In Team Fortress 2, they become part of someone's identity. A hat is not just something on a character's head. It represents time, effort, personality, and countless memories. A completely ridiculous combination of items can somehow create a character that feels more memorable than a carefully written protagonist.  And the community understands this better than anyone.  Team Fortress 2 players do not just play the game.  They create a culture around it.  They create jokes, traditions, stories, challenges, friendships, and moments that continue long after the match ends. The game became more than what was originally created because the players themselves helped build an entire world around it.  That is why TF2 refuses to disappear.  It is not alive because it is constantly trying to be something new.  It is alive because it already became something unique.  A game can be replaced.  A feeling cannot.  And the feeling of Team Fortress 2 is impossible to recreate.  It is the feeling of joining a server without knowing what will happen.  It is the feeling of laughing at something completely unexpected.  It is the feeling of a random match becoming a story you tell years later.  It is the feeling that, for a few moments, the game stopped being a game and became something much more memorable.  Team Fortress 2 is not flawless.  It was never supposed to be.  It is strange.  It is chaotic.  It is unpredictable.  It is ridiculous.  And that is exactly why it is legendary.  Because sometimes the greatest creations are not the ones that follow every rule.  Sometimes the greatest creations are the ones that break every rule, put on a ridiculous hat, pick up a ridiculous weapon, do something completely impossible, and somehow make it look perfect.  That is Team Fortress 2.  Not just a game.  Not just a classic.  A phenomenon that somehow turned chaos into art.

Now despite the thumbs up this is more so a more nuanced review of the game. It is neither going to be the most positive nor negative review ever. I'm going to give all my gripes and all my love for this game.  The thumbs up is only there specifically because I love this game, and will always love this despite the issues, however... its hard to recommend to new players.  In terms of the gameplay its already been talked about to death. The game is amazing to play, and still does so much better compared to any other FPS games I have played. The movement is amazing, the skill floor is nearly perfect where it is easy to learn, but hard to master. There is so much variety in this game where each class are designed in a way where anyone of any skill level can still play a class, and enjoy them. Some are easier and some are harder than others, and that is the overall beauty of this game in terms of gameplay. Overall this game is amazing, and the endless variety and ways of playing the game can keep you coming back.  However regarding the flaws if I were to sum up TF2's flaws in one word it would be neglect, specifically neglect from Valve from keeping this game at a good state.  For one there was the bot crisis which while gone nowadays was inexcusable and we shouldn't have left Valve get away with such a blatant problem for 8 years. However the biggest problem with TF2 is its matchmaking, this is by far the worst matchmaking I have seen in any game if I were to be honest. Unbalanced teams, Absurdly large Queue Times, Unbalanced Team Numbers, Round limits leading to shorter matches, so on and so fourth. Not to mention it is wrapped in an MMR system which prioritizes skill in a game where people play in so many ways, both in serious and especially non serious manners that it goes to the point that the MMR just cannot compute in an efficient way.  There is a movement known as Bring Back Quickplay in the TF2 sphere, where the goal is basically to bring back the old matchmaking system and while I wasn't there at the time, from the looks of it it seems better than the modern matchmaking system we have now, so if Valve did that or fix to theoretically fix matchmaking, the game could be at its best state yet.  Though that's if Valve does something. The game is barley being supported, while yes it does receive "updates" its only an excuse to bring bad cosmetics in the game, and maps that break the matchmaking even further. Yes its an old game and is pass its prime, but the issue isn't really that I want it to get back to its Golden Age or anything. That would never happen. The issue is Valve left TF2 in such a bad state of utter neglect, and I think if they at least gave the time to at least fix the matchmaking or fix issues which has plagued the game for years it would be in a better state.  In the mean time I do recommend you join Community Servers, now this isn't a perfect mainly because most Community Servers are dead and barley anyone plays these but they do exist, so you just have to look for them, and check for seeding times and such. Not only are you going to make friends within these server the overall Quality of them are way better than Valve Casual. The ruleset fits TF2 way more, and games are especially balanced because you have tools such as Team Scramble to balance out the games. Also you just get to play more TF2 due to games being determined due to Map Timers rather than Round limits. Overall the experience of playing a Community Server is just far better, and is more fun overall.  Anyway to sum up my thoughts, I love this game, but it has flaws. Valve if your reading this stop neglecting this game, and at least put in 2% of work onto this game. This would make things way better.

Okay Let start this off by saying Team Fortress 2 isn’t just a game. It’s one of the funniest, most chaotic, and downright most lively experiences I’ve ever had both in a literal sense (I, too, am a creature of flesh and blood, walking this God’s green earth) and in the sense that TF2 feels like a living, breathing entity that doesn't really feel like it should exist, but yet it does. It’s probably the most fun I’ve had in an online game in years, and that’s saying something in this current era of gaming where either feel overlyserious with certain esports titles or battle royales designed to make monetary value of your every waking moment.  TF2’s humor is what mainly sets it apart for me, and by the looks of it, otehrs feel the same way. It’s the kind of game where you and your teammates can basically spend an entire match perfecting your taunt game whether it’s synchronizing a group dance, timing the Heavy’s “POOTIS” to co exist with a perfectly placed “k” input (mapped to the kill key, because why not?), or just generally turning the battlefield into a stage for the world’s most absurd improv comedy show. The funni moments are endless, and they’re what make TF2 feel less like a game and more like a playground for creativity and laughter, which is mainly what makes it unique compared to other competitive shooting games.   Also, if I had to pick a main class, it’d be the Engineer every step of the way. Why compared to literally all the classes in the game? Because playing Engineer is like being the The Human Shield of TF2 part builder, part defender, part sitting duck if you’re not careful. There’s a certain joy to it that I haven’t found in many other classes. You’re not just another gunner on the battlefield, you’re the architect of your team’s success and the bane of the enemy’s existence.  Placing dispensers and sentry guns to hold a choke point? It's definately Stressful, but rewarding when your team pushes forward because you bought them time. Constantly scanning for Spies lurking in the shadows, ready to backstab you into oblivion? Edge of your seat stuff. Praying for an Uber Medic to swoop in and save your hard-built buildings from a Demoman’s sticky bomb trap? That’s the kind of tension that makes TF2 feel like real a high stakes thriller.  And here’s the thing, that stress isn’t unique to the Engineer. Every class in TF2 demands focus, adaptability, and a healthy dose of chaos management. Even the “simple” roles like capping a point or grabbing intelligence require split second decisions and teamwork. Sure, some classes have it easier in terms of  minimal management, but they’re all part of a symphony where every player’s actions can turn the tide of a match.  But here's the real meat and Potato's, what truly makes TF2 special though, is its community. The maps? Mostly if not all community-made. The mods? Community driven. The animations, memes, and fan creations? All born from the love of players who’ve kept this game alive for almost two decades. Valve’s decision to largely step back and let the fans take the reins speaks volumes about their true respect for the game and its community. While Valve did eventually return with new updates in 2023 after a seven year hiatus (the last major update before that was in 2016, almost a decade ago!), the fact that TF2 thrived without constant developer intervention is a testament to its design and the passion of its players.   Which is also another reason as to why it stands out from most competitive shooter titles.   I mean, just look at YouTube and search for “SFM animations” or “TF2 fan films,” and you’ll find thousands of videos featuring the game’s iconic Mercs. The sheer volume of fan content isn’t just a sign of longevity, it’s proof that TF2 isn’t just a game. It’s a cultural phenomenon that continues to inspire creativity, camaraderie, and endless laughter.  Now, let’s talk about the elephant in the room, TF2 isn’t exactly flawless. Far from it. It has its moments especially when playing Engineer that will make you want to yeet your controller across the room, and become animated like a cartoon character, all red in the face and have steam come out of your ears. The Spy, for example, is a constant PAIN IN YOUR ASS, If you main Engineer, you will develop a love hate relationship with Spy players with the amount of times they sneak up on you out of no where, stabing you in the back and destroying your buildings. Meanwhile you just have to sit and watch as all your hard work gets destroyed  while waiting to respond. Which can be extremely infuriating if you're just starting out. And then there’s the competitive mode, which, let’s be real, has its fair share of issues that even the most seasoned TF2 players can’t ignore.  But here’s the thing those flaws don’t detract from the fun to be had in the game. If anything, they make the victories much sweeter. There’s nothing quite like outplaying a Spy who’s inches away from backstabbing you, or watching your team push forward because you held the line with your sentry gun. TF2’s imperfections are part of its charm and why it still stands the test of time.  My Verdict: 8.5/10 So, where does that leave us? I’d give Team Fortress 2 a solid 8.5/10. It’s a game that’s aged pretty well, despite its flaws. What holds it back from a full 10? Well, the occasional frustrations with classes like the Spy, the wonky competitive mode, and the fact that Valve’s updates have been pretty inconsistant at best. But those issues are outweighed by everything that makes TF2 great which is, its humor, its community, its creativity, and its sheer fun times to be had.  If you haven’t played TF2 yet, do yourself a favor and go check it out because you just might end up the funniest experince of your life. And if you've already played it? You already know. You’re part of the cult. (one of us, one of us, ONE OF US)   So here are my final thoughts and honestly I could ramble about this game for hours (and honestly, I probably have). But I’ll leave it at this: Team Fortress 2 isn’t just a game you play. It’s an experience you live. One that proves sometimes, the best things in life (and gaming) are the ones that make you laugh, sweat, and cheer, all at the same time. And if you don’t have the attention span to read all this? Well, too bad. Sucks to have a small ass Gen Alpha brain like yours. :)

**Below is a note to the Tf2 Community reading this**  **I absolutely LOVE this game with its characters, charm, and timelessness. And you all do as well. But the issues that plague the game now are inexcusable. These are Valve's problems that THEY made, and it has gone on long enough.  People, put the pressure on Valve. If you have a passion for and are deeply concerned about this games legacy and integrity for the long run, speak up. Write a CONSTRUCTIVE negative review. Submit CONSTRUCTIVE complaints directly to Valve through the Tf2 website and be VOCAL. Not rude, but be loud about your disappointment with the current state of the game. And critically, OFFER UP A POTENTIAL SOLUTION that YOU think of. That is how complaints work best, pointing out a problem, but also offering up some kind of solution to that problem to show that you have thought about more than just complaining.   I know that we have the ability within us to get Valve's attention. We did it before, and by God we'll do it again if we should, which we must. Get to work people!**  End of note  There are numerous fundamental problems that make playing this game in the modern day horrible. It simply isn't up to the standard it used to have.   Here are the biggest problems to me.   1. New Player Experience is VERY Inadequate  There exist things that a player needs to change and mess with on their game so that they can play in a way that is anywhere close to fun. And none of them are things new players would even think of looking at.  Examples include: -FOV: Is set by default to 75, when in reality, the game is far more playable in 90. -Fast Weapon Switch: By default, it is turned off, and there is not an intuitive way to tell where to find the setting to enable it. Playing the game is near impossible with it off. -Lots of others  Additionally, the most amount of help new players will get on how the game actually is played, is by tips that appear while loading into a game. The existing tutorial only covers 4 out of the 9 classes in the game. Soldier, Demoman, Spy, and Engineer. And they must be completed IN THAT ORDER. Worse, these tutorials only cover the stock weapons for the classes, and do not at all explain anything about the NUMEROUS different unlockable weapons that are now in the game.  All of this must be redone to create a successful system that will properly teach new players the ropes of the game, and increase their chance of getting further into it.  Additionally, free to play accounts do not have the ability to use basic voice commands that are ESSENTIAL to good gameplay. It makes at least a hair of sense why this was done with full voice chat, but the extension of this to the regular voice commands like calling for a medic is inexcusable.   2. Matchmaking system  The current system that is used to put players into matches is very inconsistent and ridiculous.   Numerous games you will get into end up being super 1 sided, with your either steam-rolling, or being steam rolled. Good games exist, but are FAR too rare in the pool of matches you'll play.   This needs to be COMPLETELY overhauled. Get rid of the current system, figure out and test what works, and implement what does. Players need to end up in games that properly test their skills against others of similar skills, and end up being balanced to fight overall.   The current system is absolute trash.  3. Overall Facelift  The fact that the game is functionally and visually stuck in the past, may be good on the surface, but in truth, this game needs a MASSIVE functional and visual facelift. Now I don't mean the art style or character designs, as that is perfectly fine.   I mean things like: -The menu system, it can be tidied up A LOT -Graphics, aren't too bad, but could definitely be done in a more up to date way -Redundant features removed or fixed. Replay, Coaching, etc. -Achievements, some are broken and out of date, need to be removed or fixed -Etc.  All of this is to say, I LOVE this game, do not misunderstand. But I am disappointed with the amount of neglect and lack of love this game has seen in the past decade. The game was great, so why can it not be great again? The answer, it can, Valve just needs to hear us and do something. Thank you.

The Excellence of Team Fortress 2 When Maining Soldier Team Fortress 2 (TF2), developed by Valve, has long been celebrated as one of the most iconic multiplayer shooters in gaming history. Its enduring popularity stems from its unique blend of teamwork, class diversity, and fast-paced action. Among the nine playable classes, the Soldier stands out as a particularly rewarding choice for players. Maining Soldier not only highlights the strengths of TF2’s design but also provides an experience that is both accessible to beginners and deeply engaging for seasoned players.  Versatility and Reliability The Soldier embodies versatility. Equipped with a powerful rocket launcher, he can deal significant damage at both close and medium ranges. Unlike classes that specialize in narrow roles, Soldier adapts to a variety of situations: defending objectives, leading offensive pushes, or supporting teammates in critical moments. His balanced combination of offense, defense, and durability makes him one of the most reliable classes in the game.  Rocket Jumping and Mobility One of the Soldier’s defining mechanics is rocket jumping, a skill that allows players to use explosive force to propel themselves across the map. This ability transforms the Soldier from a grounded fighter into a highly mobile threat capable of surprising enemies from unexpected angles. Mastering rocket jumps requires practice and precision, but the reward is immense. It adds a creative dimension to gameplay, enabling players to explore maps in innovative ways and gain tactical advantages that other classes cannot easily replicate.  Contribution to Team Dynamics Beyond individual strength, Soldier plays a vital role in team dynamics. His high health pool allows him to absorb damage and protect more vulnerable teammates, while his rockets can clear choke points and disrupt enemy formations. Whether paired with a Medic to spearhead an assault or positioned strategically to defend objectives, Soldier’s presence often shifts the momentum of battle. His ability to balance personal performance with team contribution exemplifies the cooperative spirit of TF2.  Accessibility and Depth The Soldier is a class that bridges accessibility and depth. For newcomers, his straightforward weapon mechanics make him easy to learn: aim, fire, and deal damage. Yet for experienced players, the Soldier offers endless opportunities for mastery. Perfecting rocket aim, timing jumps, and predicting enemy movement elevate gameplay to a higher level. This balance of simplicity and complexity reflects TF2’s broader design philosophy—easy to pick up, but challenging to master.  Conclusion Maining Soldier in Team Fortress 2 is more than a personal preference; it is an experience that showcases the brilliance of the game itself. His versatility, mobility, and team impact highlight the thoughtful design choices that have made TF2 a timeless classic. Whether soaring across the battlefield with a rocket jump or leading a decisive push with teammates, Soldier ensures that every match is dynamic, exciting, and memorable. In many ways, he represents the very heart of TF2’s enduring appeal.

É com profundo rigor analítico e inequívoca seriedade que me dirijo a este espaço para expor uma das anomalias socioeconômicas mais fascinantes e alarmantes da era digital: a hiperinflação e a consequente valorização estratosférica dos bens intangíveis no ecossistema de Team Fortress 2. Ao longo dos meus anos de observação e participação ativa nos mercados digitais, testemunhei a transição de um mero passatempo eletrônico para uma complexa bolsa de valores descentralizada, cuja liquidez e valoração de ativos desafiam a lógica tradicional da escassez. Não nos detemos aqui diante de simples adornos virtuais; refiro-me a commodities digitais cujos preços de mercado superam o valor venal de veículos automobilísticos e, em casos de extrema raridade, equivalem a entradas substanciais de bens imóveis no mundo físico. A fundamentação científica para tal fenômeno repousa em três pilares perfeitamente identificáveis: 1. A Escassez Artificial Absoluta Diferente das moedas fiduciárias emitidas por bancos centrais, a emissão de determinados itens dentro do jogo — notadamente os de qualidade Unusual dotados de efeitos visuais específicos, ou as variantes de fabricação limitada como os itens Collector's — é rigidamente controlada por algoritmos probabilísticos de probabilidade ínfima. O exemplo mais crasso de minha análise manifesta-se no lendário Golden Frying Pan (Frigideira de Ouro), cujo índice de obtenção através do modo Mann Up é tão marginal que eleva seu valor de troca para patamares que orbitam entre 3.500 e 6.000 dólares americanos por unidade. 2. A Métrica de Status Sociocultural Interno A ostentação de um artefato como o Unusual Burning Flames Team Captain transcende a estética. Eu observo que tal item atua como um indexador de poder aquisitivo e prestígio dentro daquela comunidade. A validação social impulsiona a demanda de forma inelástica: quanto maior o preço, maior o desejo da elite financeira do jogo em adquiri-lo para consolidar sua posição na pirâmide hierárquica do servidor. 3. A Conversão Cambial Paralela O mercado não oficial estabeleceu uma paridade cambial com o dólar americano por meio de ativos intermediários, como as Mann Co. Supply Crate Keys (Chaves de Caixa de Suprimentos). Essa infraestrutura financeira paralela permite que investidores transacionem milhares de dólares fora do ecossistema centralizado da Valve, gerando um ambiente de especulação pura e desregulamentada. > Nota de Observação: É imperativo ressaltar que nos deparamos com um cenário onde um chapéu virtual composto por pixels tridimensionais e um efeito de fogo digital pode ser cotado a mais de 15.000 dólares. Trata-se, portanto, de uma demonstração inequívoca de que o valor não reside na matéria, mas sim na crença coletiva de sua exclusividade. >  Concluo, sob minha óptica estritamente técnica, que o mercado de bens de Team Fortress 2 deixou de ser uma economia de suporte para se tornar um estudo de caso antropológico e econômico sobre a mercantilização do supérfluo digital. Os preços praticados hoje não são apenas caros; são a manifestação terminal da especulação de luxo em ambiente virtual.  Agora vai tomar no cu enginner seu filha de uma puta mal comida

I miss what it used to be.    I put 1000 hours into this game when I bought it in 2007.  Then they flung open the floodgates and there were hats! and idle servers!  Then it became free-to-play and my $60 I spent to get the game had no meaning anymore, and it was open season for every pre-teen with time to kill to grief and screw around and no longer actually play the game.    There was no longer any prestige to having the weapons you had, for there were now about a hundred different weird little things that you could end up with.  Some of them were alright -  but as they added and added, the concept of balance was no longer a real possibility.  The fine-tuned game I knew became a mess of contraptions now more akin to some sort of joke game than a game that felt polished and competitive.  But Valve was rolling in it with the hat economy and scrap metal - it was clear which way the wind was blowing.  Slowly, I stopped playing.  I hoped maybe there would be some sort of return to form against the odds, but clearly nothing has changed in the decade since.  Oh well, I had a great time in those years before things became such a mess.  But I would not recommend this game in the form it is now.

Team Fortress 2 is a game that I have played since early 2009 (you can check my mercenary badge and achievements if you don't believe me), though my hours don't reflect that for one simple reason: after 2016, trying to play the game for any significant period of time leads to nothing but frustration and tedium. Horribly imbalanced, extremely short matches where the only solution is to wait longer and sit through more loading screens as you queue over and over again hoping for a balanced match.  Before TF2 completely screwed up their official servers, they used to have a server-wide 45 minute time limit that ensured every game mode had a fair chance to be played. Whether you wanted to play Capture the Flag, Attack/Defense, 5CP, KoTH, Payload, or even the other gamemodes, there was a consistency to every match where you knew no matter how good or poorly your team played, you would get to KEEP PLAYING, without interruption.  Speaking of teams playing poorly, there used to be Team Scrambles to help mitigate imbalanced games. These would work without having to interrupt your game with pre-game waiting and server resets. It was simple: if one team won 2 rounds in a row, it would scramble the players around between the two teams at the start of the next round, attempting to create an even points spread. You could also vote for a scramble if it looked hopeless, and there was a cooldown so you couldn't spam scrambles. In Casual, all you can do is requeue and spend even longer waiting and not actually playing or suffer through a 5 minute game.  You could also choose official Valve servers from the server browser, which is how I preferred to find games back then. Instead of waiting, hoping a game with the map you want to play on appears, you could just see for yourself if a map was being played, see its ping and player count, and decide to join it. Now, you are forced to wait in a queue for the game to "graciously allow" you into a server, when there are plenty of open and joinable servers that you would be able to click into in 5 seconds. You can actually see a list of Valve servers online, there are hundreds of them with thousands of players spread throughout them at any moment, but you still have to wait for a game for some reason.  There are other things that Valve removed from official servers too, like the ability to choose your team. You like playing offense more than defense? You could pick BLU when you joined a server, and vice versa. You wanted to duel against your friend? Switch teams. The game is unbalanced and you want to help the losing team? You could. Just the removal of this and the ability to join any server you want means almost every form of player freedom and agency has been removed from official servers since the Meet your Match update of 2016.  I haven't even mentioned yet: half the servers you join into are half-empty. Yes, you will commonly be stuck in a 2v2 or a 3v3 game with no hope of it ever filling up because people cannot find the server and join from the browser or the Quickplay server list, and the matchmaker will not place more people in for whatever reason. The only solution is to requeue and wait even longer, sitting through even more loading screens, just hoping and praying the next game won't be empty as well, and having to wait EVEN! LONGER! if that next game is poor quality.  I used to call this one of my favorite games, and it still would be if the main mode of play wasn't such a horrible, unfun slog. I love the gameplay of this game, and I love the (past) memories I've made on it, but I cannot recommend the game to any new players until Casual is gutted and the old servers are brought back. If you start playing now, you will experience nothing but horrible matches that are complete stomps, games that end before you even know what you're doing, empty servers, and LOTS and LOTS of waiting.  You'd be better off playing any other F2P game but this one, honestly, as much as it pains me to say it. At least you wouldn't have to deal with empty servers and broken matchmaking.

Team Fortress 2 is one of the most entertaining class-based shooters, featuring nine unique classes with completely different playstyles. Every class has its own mechanics and an incredibly high skill ceiling. Scout players can master advanced movement, air strafing, double jumps, and precise aim, while Spy players can perform impressive trickstabs, disguises, cloak management, and mind games to outplay opponents.  The game is filled with creative and memorable mechanics. For example, players who are set on fire by Pyro can extinguish themselves by using Jarate or Mad Milk, creating fun and unexpected gameplay moments that make every match unique.  TF2 also features an enormous collection of cosmetic items and rare item qualities, including Strange, Vintage, Genuine, Unusual, and many other collectible items that allow players to create unique loadouts and personalize their characters.  One of the biggest topics within the TF2 community is the lack of major content updates. Long periods without significant updates—such as the years between 2018 and 2022—left many players hoping for new content. Because of this, many fans jokingly say that getting a major Team Fortress 2 update feels almost like getting a new Half-Life update: rare, unexpected, and always exciting.  Despite this, the game's endless skill expression, memorable mechanics, unique item system, and humorous gameplay continue to make Team Fortress 2 one of the most beloved multiplayer games of all time.

Overall Verdict: An immortal classic that is absolute chaotic fun, but will leave you asking "What the hell is even happening?" at least ten times per match.  What You’ve Figured Out By Now (The Good):      Unmatched Personality: The 9 classes aren't just generic shooters; they are full-blown psychopaths with gold-tier voice lines. You’ve probably already fallen in love with Pyro’s muffled laughter or Scout’s arrogant trash-talk.      Easy to Learn, Impossible to Master: At 4 hours, you know Soldier shoots rockets and Medic heals. The floor is low, but the skill ceiling is somewhere in the stratosphere.      It’s Actually Free: No pay-to-win mechanics. Just pure, unadulterated skill (and luck).  What is Already Annoying You (The Bad):      The Enemy Spy: Yes, that teammate walking suspiciously behind you? It was a Spy. Get ready to be backstabbed another few hundred times before you develop "Spy-checking" paranoia.      Veteran Snipers: Some people have been playing this game since 2007. You will step out of spawn, and your head will instantly explode. Don't feel bad; that Sniper hasn't seen sunlight in a decade.      Friendly Chaos: Half the time, the server forgets it's a shooter and turns into a hat-fashion simulator where everyone is doing the Kazotsky Kick in a corner instead of pushing the payload.  Final Score: 9/10

Team Fortress 2 is what happens when Valve accidentally creates one of the greatest multiplayer shooters ever made and then leaves it in the garage for fifteen years to see if it still starts.  Remarkably, it does.  Every class has personality, every weapon feels like somebody at Valve asked, "What if this was funny instead of balanced?" and somehow it all works. Rocket jumping remains an art form, spies continue to ruin friendships, and medics still possess the confidence of people who know they're keeping the entire team alive.  Of course, TF2 isn't perfect. Bots periodically invade servers like they're auditioning for Skynet, updates arrive with the urgency of continental drift, and the economy surrounding hats has probably outperformed several real-world investments.  Yet despite its age, TF2 remains one of the easiest games to lose an entire evening to. It's chaotic, ridiculous, occasionally broken, and still more entertaining than many modern shooters trying desperately to reinvent the wheel.  A timeless classic proving that good gameplay never expires, even if the anti-cheat occasionally does.

0/10 - This game ruined my perception of humanity  I launched Team Fortress 2 expecting a lighthearted shooter. In conclusion, **Team Fortress 2** is not merely an outstanding multiplayer game—it is a landmark achievement in interactive entertainment that continues to influence game design and community-driven experiences on a global scale. "Too many changes. The golden era is gone, and so am I."  They changed way too much, and for us veteran players, it’s time to walk away. Soldier’s consecutive rocket jumps are gone. Scout’s cleaver + baseball stun combo is ruined. Spy’s trickstabs are unplayable now, and the Ambassador can no longer pull off those satisfying one-shot headshots. So many high-skill, flashy playstyles that we spent countless hours mastering were wiped out in a single update. Just like that, all our memories were erased.  I miss the good old days. I miss being a friendly Hoovy and dancing in 2Fort. I miss the rush of the beta maps, grinding bots for points, and capturing the enemy's intel. I miss the chaos of setting up an Engineer teleporter right inside the enemy base. So many core memories shared with international friends are gone now. Balloon maps are deserted, and the zombie maps are dead.  I guess it’s time for me to wake up from this childhood dream. Thank you, TF2, for being such a massive part of my youth. Across two accounts, I’ve poured countless hours into this—the game I was most obsessed with in my life. Goodbye.  I truly loved this game. Even though I’m leaving, I sincerely hope new players can still find joy in you.

Why TF2 Sucks  Do you disagree with me? I don't care. Team Fortress 2 is one of the most overrated multiplayer games ever made. People keep talking about it like it's some untouchable masterpiece that every shooter should learn from. No. It's an abandoned mess held together by nostalgia, community servers, and people remembering how good it used to be.  Let's start with updates. For years, TF2 players kept repeating the same thing: "Valve will save TF2." "The Heavy Update is coming." "Next year will be huge." And what happened? Almost nothing. Years went by and the game survived almost entirely on community-made content while Valve acted like TF2 was a forgotten science project collecting dust in the basement. At some point, you have to stop inhaling copium and accept reality. TF2 isn't being kept alive by Valve. It's being kept alive by players doing Valve's job for them.  Then there's the bot problem, which might be one of the biggest embarrassments in multiplayer gaming. For years, joining a casual server felt like rolling dice. You join a match, see a bot, start a vote kick, another bot joins, another vote kick starts, and the cycle repeats. Some matches felt like they were 75% bots and 25% actual humans. There were times when fighting robots was more common than fighting real players. The fact that this problem lasted as long as it did is ridiculous.  And then we get to balance. People love pretending TF2 is perfectly balanced because every class has a role. That's not balance. That's an excuse. Some weapons are completely useless. Some weapons are incredibly annoying. Some stay overpowered for years before anyone decides to touch them. Entire strategies can become frustrating depending on what patch you're playing. The balance often feels less like careful design and more like a museum exhibit that nobody has maintained in over a decade.  Modern updates don't help either. Players wait years hoping for meaningful gameplay additions, major balance changes, or substantial new content. Instead, they get a few cosmetics, a few taunts, maybe a map, and then the waiting starts again. It feels like waiting years for a full meal and getting handed a sticker. That's what modern TF2 updates feel like.  And yes, we need to talk about the Phlog. Who looked at Pyro and thought, "You know what this class needs? Free critical hits." The Phlog turns matches into a joke. Watching a glowing Pyro charge forward and erase entire groups of players isn't my idea of skillful game design. It's one of those weapons that makes you question whether anyone actually thought through the consequences before adding it.  The saddest part is that TF2 had everything it needed to become one of the greatest multiplayer games ever made. The art style is fantastic. The characters are memorable. The class system is iconic. The game's personality is unmatched. But none of those strengths change the reality of what TF2 became. Years of neglect, years of bot infestations, years of questionable balance decisions, and years of disappointing updates have dragged the game down.  TF2 isn't surviving because it's in great condition. It's surviving because people are emotionally attached to it. There's a difference. What you're looking at isn't a healthy multiplayer game. It's a monument to wasted potential. If you want to see what happens when an amazing foundation gets abandoned for years, play Team Fortress 2. And if you want to live in peace, don't play this game.

Words will forever fail to captivate the love I've grown and have for this game. I regret not playing it sooner or even discovering its existence but I'm more than ever grateful to be playing it now. The voicelines, mercenaries, comics, lore, fan art, the unpredictable scenarios and people you receive in each match, the source filmmakers, soundtracks, intros, the degenerates, the stupid arguments, not to forget the memories and people I've met. This game has brung out the worst and best of me, other games will never manage to obliviate the amusement I've had on this pastime, and no game will ever manage to attain the appetitious impatience and ecstasy of me rushing back home just to hop on it. Whenever I needed a distraction, it was there for me. After a horrible day? There to pat my back. Whenever I've felt lonely? There to spoon and cuddle me in bed. Maybe throw in a kiss too. Even after losing a match, or winning, I cannot be toxic after them. This game has altered me in the most positive ways, to such an extent that I may as well receive withdrawals from not engaging in it after a month. I am outright enamored with everything this game has to offer and bestow you with. Not to mention, the countless references the game has had in others? Unsurpassed. The character classes and the characters themselves captivate me. I also wanted to mention how much I love Medic and Engineer.   Team Fortress 2 will always have a special place in my heart, masterfully made, with its diversity and community. Yes, there may be bad sides to it. But in the end why waste your time focusing on the negative? When you could be playing payload in exchange, casting a votekick, or simply switching matches. I will always remember the guffaws and cackles I’ve let out on each inconvenience and flunks I’ve made. I heavily, immensely recommend this game to anyone, especially those who are new to the shooter genre. My first ever shooter game. Altogether, I really love this game, and I hope that my craze will persist indefinitely.   :)

Team Fortress 2 is a classic multiplayer first-person shooter that has remained popular for many years due to its unique class-based gameplay, distinctive art style, and high skill ceiling. Each of the nine classes has a specific role, encouraging teamwork and allowing players to develop different playstyles. The game's mechanics reward practice and experience, giving skilled players many ways to improve over time.  Despite its strengths, the game can be difficult for new players to enjoy. One of the biggest issues is the level of toxicity that can be found in some matches. New players may encounter harassment, insults, or unsportsmanlike behavior, which can make learning the game frustrating rather than enjoyable. In addition, many of the game's advanced movement and combat techniques take a significant amount of time to master, creating a steep learning curve for beginners.  Another concern is the lack of major updates. While Team Fortress 2 continues to have an active community, the game has received very little substantial new content in recent years. This has led some long-time players to feel that the game has not kept pace with modern multiplayer titles, and some ongoing issues have remained unresolved for extended periods.  Overall, Team Fortress 2 is an excellent multiplayer game with deep gameplay and a dedicated community. However, its steep learning curve, the presence of toxic behavior in some matches, and the lack of regular major updates can make it a challenging experience, particularly for new players. With my funny in-game hours aside, Team Fortress 2 is a wonderful game deserving of just a few praises: ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ACCESSIBILITY- First and foremost, TF2 is free and under 30 gigs. This accessibility is sadly rare. Today, more than 50% of kids (under 18) are either playing Roblox or Fortnite . Apart from how TF2 plays, these accessibility qualities already does so much for the games discoverability. The original art work and color choices have held the test of time. No heavy clutter UI, no unnecessary rendering, and an unbelievable amount control over graphics settings. I've been playing at 600-800fps on a Ryzen 3 and 1050TI with 8G RAM. Talk about game optimization. Being able to understand what you're looking at is critical for learning any game. Thank you, TF2 for being on Source engine.  REPLAY VALUE- Did you know Team Fortress 2 was the first game to introduce a "Deliver the Payload" objective in any first person shooter? They've nailed so many other objectives. The 9 classes are all played so differently depending on your weapon choices, the current map & its objective, team compositions, and whether you're even playing against other players in the first place. YEAH, this game also has an addictive PVE game-mode called Mann vs Machine. The list never ends. Even if you've played every vanilla map (I STILL haven't btw), the custom servers continue to provide something for everyone. I started playing TF2 in 2013 and have never seen a shortage in community-made game-modes. Things like Jump/Surf maps, Deathrun, Parkour, Prophunt, Warioware, etc. are constantly producing new maps and servers. I personally dumped over 700 hours into playing the Pyro class just for the love of a community-made game-mode called Pyro Dodgeball. I would seriously still recommend this game for someone who doesn't even play First Person Shooters. The variety and replay value of TF2 transcends what even modern games wish they could offer.  PACING- Team Fortress 2 is intuitive enough for new players to be dropped into most vanilla game-modes and still have a general idea of what to do and where to go. The pacing is also superb at introducing new weapons. The pace is controlled through this game's random item drop system. With regular playtimes of 10hrs/week, it's not uncommon for the game to give you 7-10 (up to 12) weapons or cosmetics per week. This helps tremendously at pacing the learning curve in a way that's not daunting. All weapons are abundant and cheap by design. Any player could technically buy every weapon at once for less than $5, but most people don't, The random item drop system is effective enough to help pace player experience and skill at a reasonable learning rate. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- This game is by no means perfect. Let's address some negatives: ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- DEFAULT SETTINGS- Many games offer Steam guides and YouTube videos with recommended settings before even touching the game. This is sadly one of those games. Please take some time to research to get the most out of your experience. Some things are obvious to toggle while other options feel completely hidden. Even changing your desired FOV will likely require a YouTube video tutorial. Saving settings can also be a challenge as some settings don't save and carry over to your next session. Many players resort to making external files for the game to reference. These "Auto executable" files force certain settings to stay active upon every session's start. Not even TF2's volume in mixer level remains the same between sessions.  MATCHMAKING- Team Fortress 2 has incredible skill ceilings & an unbelievable amount of expression. This is true, but at times, that expression feels contingent on whether you "got lucky" with the team you joined. TF2's matchmaking algorithm takes absolutely ZERO consideration for anyone's skill, KDR stats, XP level, playtime, or class preference. This sometimes causes one-sided stomps. The lack of a proper matchmaking algorithm is also true for TF2's "Competitive" mode. Because of this, many competitive players seek external websites to help coordinate matches that are more fair; even going so far as to have ranked leagues and set teammates. This is honestly a small percentage of TF2 players.  UPDATES AND CONTENT- It's been almost 10 years since there's been anything substantial added to TF2 such as a new weapon or any major balance patches. At this point, it's a known meme that TF2 has only 6 "active" developers. Because of this, community-made updates are becoming more and more  commonplace. Many argue these community-updates are negatively impacting TF2's "classic aesthetical charm". Their argument is that a lot of what's produced is "saturated cosmetic slop" and detracts away from a style that so many of us grew up on. This portion of the review isn't for me to take a side, but rather for me to explain the divide. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- I see myself playing Team Fortress 2 for years to come.  I'm in love with the friends I've made, experiences I've shared, items I've collected, and the skill expression I've developed. I appreciate the time you've taken to read this review. I hope you develop a similar attachment. I also hope you can create unforgettable memories that'll leave impressions for the years to come. Team Fortress 2 has truly been one of those impactful games for me.

I'll disregard the grievances I have outside of the gameplay for a moment and treat this like a gameplay review. If anyone is reading this who still hasn't played the game yet, here you go. Team Fortress 2 is way different than a lot of shooters. If you've played other team based shooters like Marvel Rivals, don't expect it to be anything like that. In fact, completely disregard your view of other team based shooters for a moment. The game that comes closest to feel is probably Overwatch, but it's still way different, it's far from the same in most ways. This game is quite unique. There are nine different characters to use, which might seem daunting with how differently they all play, but you'll quickly get used to everything regarding them. They're all fun in completely different ways. Heavy? Slow, but powerful. Having a heavy can push the enemy team back with presence alone. Scout? Fast but vulnerable. You can provide meaningful chip damage to the enemy for your team and get meaningful kills on the front lines. Each class has its purpose and people enjoy them all differently. I like being supportive and helping my teammates keep up the pressure with medic, but I also enjoy engineer. In terms of the game modes? All of them can be fun, but some game modes have worse maps than others. I like payload the most, I recommend it over the other game modes but it's just my personal preference. It's hard to describe everything, but I just really like this game.   Now onto the other things, I'll be honest, this game needs a little more attention from the developers. I like that they fixed a major bug that the game had the other day...but it took literally years for it to be fixed. I hope that's not a huge ask. To be honest, I love this game. I love the community too, it's one of the biggest reasons I actually still play or boot up the game when I do. I've spent a lot of time in here because I've had a lot of good experiences with people, and I like playing medic and being a helpful teammate when it's needed. And most people appreciate that and MOST people aren't douches. Although sometimes I still get kicked for not getting enough kills or performing in the same way my teammates want me to even when I'm just minding my own, but there are people like that in every shooter I've played. I just want this game to receive a bit more love from those who maintain it. That's all. And the fact it took them so many years to fix the bot problem is an indicator of the fact that it needs a little more love and attention. But it's still an amazing game and it could be much worse. Play this game. It is very fun.

This game is a testament to excellent and intuitive game design. Does that mean the game is perfect? No. But, that doesn't negate the fact that this is a terrific game.   If you are a fan of chaotic team based shooters then this is a wonderful pick. The nine classes offer varying ways to play. So you can either play one dedicated play style or you can change it up with styles ranging from serious to silly. Support classes like medic and engineer if that is more up your alley. Sniper, spy, and scout if you like to go for more picks than anything. And then you have heavy, demoman, soldier, and pyro for devastating damage. The myriad of mpas provide plenty of scenery for the outrageous battles you'll find yourself in. And if you don't liek the maps in the queue selection, you can find plenty of communities in the community server search.  If you are also more of a PvE person, you can entrench yourself in waves of robot mercenaries with tower defense-esque upgrades. I prefer playing this mode with friends since playing with randos launches you into a roulette of sweats who may kick you for one single mistake or people who are just antagonistic to the goal of the game. And if you want more of a challenge or more ridiculous maps/enemies, there are superb community servers as well.  I have pumped more than a decade inthis game, meeting lifelong friends and solidifying my love for the FPS genre. If you want a silly game with lots of variety, unique artstyle, and something to relax with frineds to then this game is for you.

The famous Team Fortress 2. I have been exposed to the content of this game for a long time, since I started watching the internet when I was small. I finally decided to give in to the voices and actually play. So what do I have to say about this game?  For the positives, I think this game is incredible. Not oversaturated like others of its kind. It's simple and clean, with a lovable art style. To this day it has a loyal community that shows how much it cares. The characters are unique and well-written, and I never get tired of the interactions. Maps are good in general, with a few here and there that hurt my head a bit because of the way they're made, but it is alright. And classes have fun cosmetics and distinct weapons  that not only look different but also work differently.   As good as this game is, there are a few bad things to mention. The game is abandoned, fully. And no, cosmetic crates and events do not count. People always gravitate towards the same maps, so when I try a new one, I end up fighting alone with a random person and we end up dancing in the end from boredom. The matches are always horribly unbalanced. Early levels end up fighting people with WAAAY too many levels, which makes the matches unfair and frustrating. The bots appear in random matches and kick everyone out; they are unbearable, but luckily I only had  that problem once.   In conclusion, I am having a lot of fun with this game and I will keep playing it until i master it. I love the vibe of the community and the content in the game itself, even though it has its problems.

There's so much, TOO MUCH, even that can be said in regards to TF2, most of which I feel already has. But if I'm to sum it up as concisely as possible:  There have been MANY ups and downs with this game in both its history, and MY history with the game, but as it stands now. In an industry that tends to favor multiplayer shooters with more focuses on obtuse abilities, limiting player choice, and a MASSIVE focus on competitive gaming, it's REALLY nice to still have a game like TF2 where I can log in, get placed god knows where, maybe some map I haven't seen since 2015, try some objectively dumb garbage (individual performance isn't critical), and witness my team and the enemy team display some of the most erratic behavior known to man. I definitely think nostalgia has a bit of a play here, but I do still feel after all this time that this game is really something special, and worth treasuring in modern day.

Look, it's been years since I played TF2 regularly. I was really into this game over a decade ago. High quality vanilla community servers were this game's bread and butter, and Valve's own servers at the time had at least sane settings: match timers, autobalance, a curated selection of high quality maps. Now I log in and the community servers are gone, replaced by endless ctf_ ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on maps somehow worse than 2fort and others with falling hazards just outside spawn room doors or sightlines that draw the player's eye toward dead ends or the wrong way of a one-way passage.  I was trying to introduce a friend to the game recently, and we kept getting such awful matchmaking through the casual queue that we switched to Mann vs. Machine.  The state of matchmaking in this game is unconscionably bad. All but one PVP round we played last night featured a death spiral: high-performing squad carries team A while team B gets the snot beaten out of them. Half of team B requeues or quits, and quickplay can't backfill them fast enough, resulting in what is effectively an unwinnable 12v6 for team B until team A scores enough to start a map vote. We were on team A one time, and on team B for the rest of the matches before we switched to MvM.  I was unable to actually use the map vote feature. Clicking on the map options did nothing and there were no keyboard prompts. My friend is patient and understanding and willing to play more MvM, but if this had been my first time playing TF2, unassisted by a veteran player, I would have nuked the game from my hard drive faster than you can say "need a dispenser here".  Any further forays into PVP on my part will be using the "legacy" server browser only. I would rather fellate a pipe grenade than continue to use the queues.

The setting of TF2 is heavily entrenched in an absurd, alternate-history 1968. Upon his death, wealthy patriarch Zepheniah Mann leaves his useless American land empire to his two bickering sons, Redmond and Blutarch. Both sons hire private armies—Builders League United (BLU) and Reliable Excavation Demolition (RED)—to wage an endless war over the worthless gravel pits.  The roster is divided into three categories, each bringing vastly different abilities to the battlefield.  Offense Scout: A fast-talking, Boston-born baseball fan. He is the fastest class, possesses a double-jump, and captures control points twice as fast as other classes. Soldier: A jingoistic, trigger-happy patriot. Armed with a rocket launcher, he can sacrifice health to "rocket jump" into the air, allowing him to reach high vantage points. Pyro: A mysterious, pyromaniac gas-mask-wearing individual. The Pyro excels in close-range combat using a flamethrower that deals damage over time and an "airblast" capable of reflecting projectiles and extinguishing burning teammates.  Defense Demoman: A drunken explosives expert from the Scottish Highlands. Armed with a grenade launcher and stickybomb launcher, he can set devastating traps for his enemies. Heavy: A gentle giant from the USSR with a PHD in Russian literature. He is the slowest class in the game, but boasts the highest health pool and dishes out massive sustained damage via his trusty minigun. Engineer: A soft-spoken but highly intelligent Texan. He supports his team by constructing buildings: defensive Sentry Guns, health/ammo-dispensing Dispensers, and Teleporters.  Support Medic: A mad German doctor who heals wounded teammates with his Medi Gun, granting temporary invulnerability through an "ÜberCharge." Sniper: A quiet, professional outdoorsman from New Zealand. His sniper rifle allows for precise, long-range critical hits. Spy: A sophisticated French saboteur. He can cloak himself to become invisible, disguise himself as enemy players, and instantly kill opponents with backstabs.  TF2 offers a wide array of objective-based game modes, with several staples: Control Points: Teams fight to capture sequential or simultaneous points on the map. Payload: One team escorts a cart loaded with explosives through enemy territory while the other tries to stall them. Capture the Flag (CTF): Teams must infiltrate the enemy base, steal their intelligence (briefcase), and return it to their own base. King of the Hill: Both teams fight over a single, central control point, racing to hold it for a cumulative three minutes.  Beyond its shooting, TF2 is famous for being one of the pioneers of the cosmetic and in-game economy model. Random Critical Hits: In casual play, standard weapons have a chance to randomly deal triple damage, adding an element of chaos. Weapon Loadouts: Instead of just stock weapons, players can equip various unlockable weapons that change how a class plays (e.g., trading heavy health for high-speed mobility). Cosmetics & Taunts: The game popularised "hats" and in-game cosmetics, boasting a sprawling trading and digital economy (including Strange, Unusual, and Killstreak weapon tiers).  Overall, Team Fortress 2 is a great game, I do recommend it

This just isn't sustainable, TF2 with the current matchmaking has no future, only a bleak fall into irrelevence as old players give up and new players get frustrated and leave. Team Fortress 2 needs no introduction as a masterclass in game design and one of the greatest multiplayer shooters of all time. I returned to the game recently after feeling particularly nostalgic for the fun I had with it when I regularly played it in the early 2010s.  Unfortunately, I don't think it's worth playing at this time, if only for the fact that its now seemingly unmoderated community is spoiled by its innumerable bad apples. Every casual match feels like a coin toss to witness or experience some form of abuse or harassment beyond a threshold that I can accept, even in the context of an online game, as not even the lowest-hanging fruit are systematically dealt with. Avoiding the use of the in-game text or voice chat, a precautionary measure that shouldn't even be necessary in a game centered around teamwork, is not enough to spare you from this, as especially toxic players will exploit everything from item customization, to Steam community integration, to votekicks in an attempt to reach you. It's actually baffling sometimes just how randomly players will get targeted after joining a match and doing literally nothing but playing the game normally, let alone if they do anything that could be considered drawing attention to themselves.  It's tragic, but whether you're an older player considering a return to a former favorite or a fresh face considering a new-old game to get into, you really can do a lot better than TF2 these days.

Team Fortress 2 is a class-based shooter from Valve, released back in 2007. It is still alive, completely free, and absolutely fantastic. No pay-to-win. Just pure, chaotic, hilarious fun.  The game features nine unique classes. Scout is fast and loud. Soldier flies with rockets. Pyro burns everything. Demoman lays sticky bombs. Heavy is a tank with a sandwich. Engineer builds turrets and teleporters. Medic heals and grants invincibility. Sniper picks enemies from afar. Spy disguises and backstabs. Every class feels different, and the balance is still perfect after nearly 20 years.  What makes TF2 so good? The art style – bright, cartoonish, full of personality. The community – thousands of custom maps and modes. The gameplay – easy to learn, endlessly deep to master. Matches are fast, loud, and unpredictable. You will laugh as much as you fight.  Yes, the game is old. Yes, there are some bots sometimes. Yes, Valve updates it rarely. But none of that matters. Team Fortress 2 is one of the best multiplayer shooters ever made.  Final verdict: If you have never played it – download it right now. It is free on Steam, runs on any computer, and will give you hundreds of hours of genuine fun. I cannot recommend Team Fortress 2 in its current state. The game still has small moments of fun, but they are buried under years of neglect. Performance is bad, with constant micro-lags, freezes, and random stutters. Casual matchmaking is often unbalanced, and if you queue with friends, you can easily end up joining a team that is already losing because half the server left. Autobalance can also split you from your party, which makes the experience even more frustrating.  The anti-cheat and moderation are also in a terrible state. VAC feels ineffective, reporting players barely seems to matter, and there is almost no visible moderation for griefing, toxicity, or people ruining matches. A lot of servers feel like complete chaos, with players doing whatever they want and no clear structure or control. Community servers can sometimes be better, but there are not enough good ones, and many of the enjoyable servers have high ping depending on where you live. The result is that maybe 5% of the game is still genuinely enjoyable, but you may need to waste hours just to get one decent match.  The community is also a major problem. There are still good players, of course, but a large part of the experience is toxic chat, random kicks, strange “unspoken rules,” and people with thousands of hours making the game miserable for newer or casual players.  At times, it feels less like a proper multiplayer game and more like a browser chatroom with a shooter running in the background.  The recent official promotion of a Moscow LAN in 2026 also made me lose even more respect for how this game is handled. Promoting an event in Russia while the war against Ukraine is still ongoing feels completely tone-deaf and disrespectful. Seeing people in the comments mock Ukrainians, post pro-war symbols, or treat the situation like a joke makes it even worse. This is not “just gaming” when the official promotion gives visibility to that kind of environment.  TF2 had a lot of potential and still has a unique style, but right now it feels like an abandoned project kept alive mostly by nostalgia and a small number of good community servers. The best way to enjoy it is probably on a private server with friends or bots. As a public online game, I honestly think it is not worth your time.  There are better ways to spend your time and money on Steam. Avoid this game unless you already know exactly what you are getting into.

I played this game for a few hours after I bought it and I didn't enjoy my time. After coming back to it a few months later I rediscovered a hidden gem in my library and I can confidently say that Team Fortress 2 has earned it's place as the best game I've ever personally played.  The game play in Team Fortress 2 is unlike anything that I've ever played. You can feel like the most powerful creature in the game while still knowing that you are only one mistake away from dying. The game is difficult in an unfair way that can initially be very frustrating as it feels that you have no control over your environment. One of the best parts of this game is it's unpredictability. Due to the fact that everything is happening at once, it really makes you feel like you're just an observer in a real world. The people in this game is really good and helps the feeling of an actual world with both friends and foes.  You play this game as a creature known as a mercenary. The best feeling in this game is the feel of getting stronger, not just from in-game upgrades or weapons, but from your skill increasing and learning new mechanics and techniques with the tools available to you. The movement in this game is very nuanced, which leads to the movement sometimes feeling unnatural or clunky, but then as you learn new movement techniques the movement becomes far more fluid and natural, which leads to some of the best feeling movements in a game that I've ever played.  There's so much more to this game that I haven't covered here, but I'll leave that up to you to decide if you would like to try the game and become more familiar with it. This game is truly one-of-a-kind and itself is an experience. It certainly isn't for everyone but it is so unique and enjoyable that if you can make it past the first few hours of game play and get the game to "click" with you, then you may just find one of the best gaming experiences that you've ever had.

Titanfall 2 is one of those games that tries hard to be impressive and mostly ends up feeling like it’s showing off without much payoff.  The campaign is probably the biggest offender. It’s short, uneven, and leans too heavily on gimmicks like the time-shifting level instead of building a strong, consistent story or memorable characters. The relationship between the pilot and the Titan is supposed to be the emotional core, but it never really lands—everything feels rushed, like it’s ticking boxes rather than telling a meaningful story.  Multiplayer doesn’t fully save it either. Movement is flashy, but it can feel chaotic and unfocused, especially for new players. Matches often swing wildly, and there’s a learning curve that feels more punishing than rewarding. On top of that, the balance between Titans and pilots can feel awkward, with certain loadouts or strategies dominating instead of encouraging variety.  Even the hype around “fluid traversal” wears off after a while, because maps sometimes feel built more for spectacle than for solid competitive flow.  Overall, it’s a game with big ideas that don’t always come together cleanly. It has moments where it shines, but as a complete package, it feels uneven and overpraised.

I love Team Fortress 2 with a devotion so irrationally intense it feels less like appreciation and more like some ancient curse branded directly into my nervous system, because no other game on this earth has ever captured the beautiful, idiotic chaos of humanity quite like it. I love the screaming madness of rockets filling the air while a crazed doctor heals a burning man sprinting headfirst into certain death with a shovel raised like a conquering king. I love the sound of distant sentries locking onto some poor fool who turned the corner half a second too late. I love the spies weaving through enemy lines with all the confidence of master assassins only to be exposed by a paranoid pyro spraying fire into literally every hallway because trust itself has long since died on these battlefields. Every match feels like civilization collapsing in real time under the weight of explosives, bad decisions, and weaponized stupidity, and it is magnificent. The mercenaries are not heroes. They are lunatics, monsters, failures, washed-up killers, mad scientists, and unhinged patriots held together by duct tape and violence, yet somehow they feel more alive than entire casts from other games combined. I love the arrogance of the Soldier, the horrifying joy of the Pyro, the endless confidence of the Scout, the cold professionalism of the Sniper, the Engineer building miracles from scrap metal while chaos detonates around him like the wrath of God itself. I love how a single second can transform triumph into catastrophe: an Übercharge shattered by a random crit, a perfect defense destroyed by one drunk demoman flying through the sky screaming incomprehensibly before detonating half the team into red mist. And through all of it there is laughter, endless laughter, because Team Fortress 2 understands something few games ever have: war is horrifying, but people are ridiculous, and when you combine the two you create something immortal. I have seen entire teams stop fighting just to dance together while rockets and grenades explode around them like fireworks celebrating collective insanity. I have seen friendships formed in the middle of absolute digital slaughter. I have seen communities survive for years fueled entirely by memes, rage, hats, and an almost religious refusal to let the game die. Other games strive for realism, for balance, for perfection, but Team Fortress 2 thrives in glorious imperfection, in the unpredictable symphony of screaming voices, missed shots, miraculous plays, and catastrophically bad ideas somehow succeeding anyway. I do not merely play it. I return to it like a man returning to the ruins of a beloved city, broken and ancient and beautiful beyond explanation, because somewhere beneath the noise and madness and absurdity is a soul unlike anything else ever made.

If you’ve ever wondered whether TF2 is worth jumping into in 2026, let me say this as clearly as I can: yes. Absolutely yes. Do yourself a favor and play it. This game isn’t just a shooter — it’s a piece of gaming history that somehow still feels alive, still feels welcoming, and still feels like home every time you boot it up.  I’ve played a lot of games over the years, but TF2 is one of the few that never loses its charm. There’s something magical about how simple it looks on the surface, yet how deep and endlessly replayable it becomes once you’re in the thick of it. Every class has personality, every map has memories, and every match feels like a tiny story unfolding in real time.  What makes TF2 special is the community energy. Even after all these years, you’ll find players who just want to have fun — people who crack jokes in chat, dance on the payload, build goofy Engineer nests, or charge into battle with a Market Garden attempt that absolutely should not work but somehow does. It’s chaotic, it’s ridiculous, and it’s perfect.  The art style is timeless. The humor is iconic. The gameplay is smooth in a way modern shooters still struggle to match. And the best part? You can play however you want.   Want to sweat and top‑frag? Go for it. Want to chill and build a sentry farm? Totally valid. Want to rocket jump until your hands hurt? Welcome home.  TF2 is one of those rare games that grows with you. When you’re new, it’s goofy fun. When you’re experienced, it becomes a playground of skill, creativity, and pure momentum. And even after hundreds of hours, you’ll still find new tricks, new strategies, and new moments that make you laugh.  If you’re on the fence, let me say this from the heart: TF2 is worth your time. It’s worth the download, worth the matches, worth the memories you’ll make along the way. It’s a game that doesn’t just entertain — it sticks with you.  I absolutely recommend this game 100%. TF2 isn’t just a classic — it’s a comfort game, a community, and a little slice of gaming joy that refuses to fade.

Team Fortress 2 is not just another multiplayer shooter to me — it’s one of the greatest video games ever created. Even after all these years, the game still feels alive, fun, and unique in a way that most modern games fail to achieve. TF2 has a soul. From the iconic art style to the unforgettable characters, music, voice acting, maps, and chaotic gameplay, everything about this game has personality. Instead of trying to look “realistic” like every other shooter, TF2 created its own timeless style, and that’s exactly why it aged so well. Every class feels memorable and full of life. The Scout is fast, annoying, and hilarious. The Soldier is pure chaos. The Heavy somehow became one of the most lovable characters in gaming history. The Spy makes you feel like a genius when your plans actually work. No class feels boring, and every character has their own charm, playstyle, and identity. TF2 didn’t just make classes — it made legends. One of the best things about TF2 is the freedom it gives players. You can play competitively and take the game seriously, or you can join a random server and spend hours laughing at dumb moments, dancing with strangers, or fighting in complete chaos. Few games can balance skill, comedy, teamwork, and randomness this perfectly. Every match creates new memories, funny moments, and stories you’ll remember years later. The community is another reason why TF2 is special. Even after such a long time, the community is still active, passionate, creative, and loyal. Players continue making maps, mods, animations, memes, cosmetics, fan art, and videos because they genuinely love the game. TF2 feels less like a product and more like a giant creative world built by both the developers and the players together. What makes TF2 truly legendary is its design. The gameplay is easy to understand but incredibly deep to master. Every class has strengths, weaknesses, and unique mechanics that reward skill and creativity. You can spend hundreds or even thousands of hours improving and still learn something new. That kind of game design is rare. TF2 also influenced an entire generation of multiplayer games. So many hero shooters tried to copy what TF2 did, but very few understood what made it special in the first place. TF2 was never just about abilities or classes — it was about personality, freedom, humor, and unforgettable gameplay. It has a charm that no other game has been able to truly replicate. No matter how many new games come out, Team Fortress 2 will always remain one of the most iconic, creative, and entertaining games ever made. It’s more than just a shooter — it’s a piece of gaming history, and honestly, a masterpiece.
